title: Abbas ibn Firnas
hook: a craftsman of Cordoba who, the reports say, strapped on wings and jumped

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abd al-Rahman the Third, the ruler in Cordoba who took the title of caliph. Your line was: a western caliphate. Did you stop to think about what a golden age costs, and who pays it? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

A man stands on a high place near Cordoba. Feathers are fastened over his body, and a pair of wings is tied to his arms. People have come out to watch. He leans forward, and he jumps. That is how a later historian of al-Andalus, al-Maqqari, tells it, passing on what earlier writers said they saw. The man glides for a stretch, the report says, the way a bird does. Then he comes down hard, and hurts his back. His name was Abbas ibn Firnas, and today belongs to him.
screen: `FEATHERS AND A PAIR OF WINGS.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `HE COMES DOWN HARD.`

segments.voice: Who was he? In the reports, a man of the Cordoba court with many crafts at once: poetry, music, the stars, the making of instruments. The same writers credit him with work on glass made from stone, and with a model of the sky built in his own house. Take those as the reports give them, admiring and a little larger than life. Now the birds. The Qur'an keeps sending its listeners outside to look. In Pickthall's translation: "Have they not seen the birds above them spreading out their wings and closing them?" The verse goes on to say that nothing holds them up except the Beneficent. So looking up at a bird, in this tradition, is already a kind of reading. Abbas looked, and then he tried. Here is the detail worth carrying home. Why did he land so badly? The report has an answer, and it's oddly specific. He had forgotten that birds come down on their tails, so he never made himself one. He studied the wing and missed the tail. A very human mistake: you copy the part you admire and skip the part that looks boring. One honest caution. This is a story told long after, by a writer gathering older accounts. Some readers take it nearly as written; others wonder how much grew in the telling. Nobody can stand on that hill and check. What the story keeps, either way, is a man who wondered about birds, built something, jumped, got hurt, and left behind a lesson about tails. The fall is the part of his story that gets retold. He tried to fly.
screen: `A MAN OF MANY CRAFTS.` · `HAVE THEY NOT SEEN THE BIRDS?` · `HE FORGOT THE TAIL.` · `A REPORT, TOLD LONG AFTER.` · then, large: `HE TRIED TO FLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to attempt something new. Settle, and breathe. Let one small thing come to mind that you've never tried. A dish, a stretch, a phrase in another language, a route home, a question you've never asked someone. Keep it small enough to do today. Now picture the first step, only the first one. Then ask the Abbas question: what's my tail? What dull part am I likely to skip? Muslims often say bismillah, in the name of God, before beginning something. If you pray, you can begin your attempt with it. If you don't, just hold the first step in mind. The bell holds the time.
At-tayr. Arabic for the birds, the Qur'an's call to look up, which Abbas ibn Firnas answered by putting on wings, jumping, gliding, and landing hard for want of a tail. Today's word.
Your line: he tried to fly. Today, try one new thing small enough to finish before bed, and afterward name one thing you'd change next time. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Abbas ibn Firnas is remembered as an inventor of al-Andalus, and his attempted flight is known mainly through the account passed on by the historian al-Maqqari.

fork.setup: you're Abbas, on the high place near Cordoba. the wings are tied on, the crowd is watching. what does the report say happens next?
options: he looks down, unties the wings and walks home.
he jumps, glides a stretch, and lands hard.
he flies over the city and back without a scratch.
fork.reveal: he jumps, glides for a stretch like a bird, and comes down hard enough to hurt his back. the report's explanation: he forgot the tail.
